name: Ectoin

lead: Ectoin is a small molecule that salt-loving bacteria make to survive harsh conditions. Skincare brands use it in moisturisers and sun-care products for hydration, soothing and UV-stress protection.
Support comes mostly from lab studies in cells; a hydration and barrier trial in eczema is registered, and other ectoin products have been tested for airway, nasal and eye conditions.

paras: It is described as a compatible solute that organises water around proteins and membranes and stabilises them; the 2004 cell study reported it limited several UVA-induced damage signals.
The sources reviewed describe it as well tolerated in nasal-spray use and report no specific skin safety concerns; formal safety data for cosmetic use are limited in the sources reviewed.

lead: Ectoin (also spelled ectoine) is a small, water-soluble amino acid derivative produced by many bacteria that live in salty or otherwise stressful environments. It acts as a 'compatible solute', protecting cells from osmotic stress, and has been commercialised as a cosmetic and medical-device ingredient for skin soothing, hydration and UV-related protection.[1]

In laboratory work, a 2004 study in cultured skin cells reported that ectoin reduced several markers of UVA-induced cell damage.[2] A registered human trial has examined a 7 percent ectoin dermatitis cream for skin hydration and barrier function in atopic dermatitis, and other ectoin products have been studied for airway, nasal and eye conditions.[3][4]
Ectoin is discussed mainly as a barrier-calming ingredient in skincare. No published trial has tested it for improving facial appearance in healthy people.
infobox: Bacteria such as Halomonas elongata; produced industrially by fermentation[1]
Topical; also nasal, eye and inhaled products
Sold over the counter in the EU in some medical-device products[1]

paras: Ectoin was first identified in the bacterium Ectothiorhodospira halochloris and later found in many Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. It is a white powder with a molar mass of about 142 g/mol, made in three enzymatic steps from aspartic beta-semialdehyde.[1] Bacteria from salty, arid and marine habitats are a common source of such solutes.[5]
According to Wikipedia, the molecule stabilises proteins and structures water around them, and has been reported to protect DNA from radiation by scavenging free radicals.[1]
Ectoin is used in moisturisers, after-sun and sun-protection products and barrier creams, where manufacturers market it for skin hydration and protection against dryness and UV stress.[1][2]

In Europe, ectoin is used in nasal sprays, eye drops, lozenges and inhalation solutions for allergic and inflammatory conditions, and a nasal spray was reported as comparable to cromoglycate and well tolerated.[1] A US drug label on DailyMed lists a topical product combining glycerin, lidocaine and ectoin 0.12 percent for haemorrhoid and fissure use.[6]

A registered study of an ectoin dermatitis cream 7 percent assessed skin hydration and barrier function in 35 people with atopic dermatitis; no published results are listed.[3] Other registered ectoin studies include a randomised trial of inhaled ectoin on neutrophilic lung inflammation in older adults, which reported reduced inflammation markers,[7] a post-market study of ectoin inhalation solution in asthma,[8] a placebo-comparison of allergy nasal spray and eye drops,[4] and observational studies in rhinosinusitis.[9]

Skin-appearance evidence in healthy people is limited to laboratory work: the 2004 study used cell cultures and other bench methods and reported that ectoin counteracted several UVA-induced cellular changes.[2] A 2008 study compared ectoin, ergothioneine and mannitol with sunscreens in assessing visible-light genotoxicity.[10] Animal work also reported reduced nanoparticle-induced lung inflammation.[11]
